title: If you have N instances, how do you distribute requests equally (load balancer algorithms, health checks, Kubernetes Service)?
shortTitle: If you have N instances, how do you distribute requests equally

s1_definition.profdef: Distributing requests equally across N instances is the job of a load balancer, which applies a balancing algorithm to decide which instance handles each request. Common algorithms are round-robin (rotate through instances in order), least-connections (send to the instance with the fewest active requests), weighted variants (bias toward more powerful instances), and consistent hashing (route by a key so the same client or key sticks to the same instance). Health checks ensure only healthy instances are in the rotation, and in Kubernetes a Service plus kube-proxy provides this balancing automatically across the healthy Pod endpoints behind a stable virtual address.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India has several identical counters open and a crowd of customers arriving. A receptionist at the door decides who goes to which counter so that no single clerk is overwhelmed while others sit idle. The simplest fair rule is to send people to counters in rotation, one each in turn (round-robin). A smarter rule is to look at which counter currently has the shortest queue and send the next person there (least-connections). If one counter has a faster, more experienced clerk, you can send them a larger share (weighted). And for customers who need their ongoing paperwork, you might always send the same customer to the same clerk who knows their case (consistent hashing). Throughout, the receptionist only directs people to counters that are actually open and staffed (health checks), never to a closed one.
s1_definition.oneliner: A load balancer spreads requests across N healthy instances using an algorithm like round-robin or least-connections, health checks keep dead instances out of the rotation, and a Kubernetes Service does all of this automatically behind a stable address.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Distributing requests equally across N instances is the job of a load balancer, which applies a balancing algorithm to decide which instance handles each request. Common algorithms are round-robin (rotate through instances in order), least-connections (send to the instance with the fewest active requests), weighted variants (bias toward more powerful instances), and consistent hashing (route by a key so the same client or key sticks to the same instance). Health checks ensure only healthy instances are in the rotation, and in Kubernetes a Service plus kube-proxy provides this balancing automatically across the healthy Pod endpoints behind a stable virtual address.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India has several identical counters open and a crowd of customers arriving. A receptionist at the door decides who goes to which counter so that no single clerk is overwhelmed while others sit idle. The simplest fair rule is to send people to counters in rotation, one each in turn (round-robin). A smarter rule is to look at which counter currently has the shortest queue and send the next person there (least-connections). If one counter has a faster, more experienced clerk, you can send them a larger share (weighted). And for customers who need their ongoing paperwork, you might always send the same customer to the same clerk who knows their case (consistent hashing). Throughout, the receptionist only directs people to counters that are actually open and staffed (health checks), never to a closed one.

**One line to remember:** A load balancer spreads requests across N healthy instances using an algorithm like round-robin or least-connections, health checks keep dead instances out of the rotation, and a Kubernetes Service does all of this automatically behind a stable address.

sections.s2_technical:
The fundamental idea is that a load balancer sits in front of N identical instances and, for each incoming request, selects one instance according to a configured algorithm. The goal is to spread work evenly so no instance is saturated while others are idle, which maximizes throughput and keeps latency low. This only works cleanly when the instances are stateless and interchangeable, because then any instance can serve any request.

Round-robin is the simplest algorithm: it cycles through the instances in order, giving each the next request in turn. It is fair when requests are uniform and instances are identical. Its weakness is that it ignores how busy each instance actually is, so if one request happens to be very slow, round-robin will still keep handing that instance new work. For example, with three instances, requests go to instance one, two, three, one, two, three, and so on.

Least-connections improves on this by sending each new request to the instance currently handling the fewest active connections or requests. This adapts to uneven request costs, because an instance stuck on a slow request accumulates connections and is skipped until it catches up. It is usually the better default for workloads with variable request durations, which most real systems have. Weighted variants of both algorithms let you bias the distribution, for example weighted round-robin sends twice as many requests to an instance that has twice the capacity, which is useful in a mixed fleet.

Consistent hashing is a different category used when you need affinity, meaning the same key should map to the same instance. You hash a key such as a user id or account id and map it to an instance on a hash ring, so that user's requests consistently land on the same instance, which helps local caching and sticky sessions. Its signature benefit is that when an instance is added or removed, only a small fraction of keys remap rather than everything reshuffling, which is why it is used for distributed caches and sharded routing. The trade-off is that it can distribute slightly unevenly if keys are skewed.

Health checks are essential to make distribution safe. The load balancer periodically probes each instance, and any instance failing the check is removed from the rotation so no traffic is sent to it, then added back when it recovers. Without this, equal distribution would blindly include dead instances and fail a share of requests. This is the same readiness concept that keeps warming-up instances out of rotation until they can serve.

In Kubernetes this is largely automatic. A Service provides a stable virtual IP and DNS name, and it tracks the set of healthy Pod endpoints via readiness probes. kube-proxy programs the node's networking so that requests to the Service IP are spread across those endpoints, effectively giving you round-robin-style balancing at the connection level without any application code. For richer algorithms like least-connections, weighted routing, or layer-seven awareness, you place an ingress controller or a service mesh in front, where the mesh sidecar can apply least-request balancing and per-route policies. The senior-level nuance is that connection-level balancing, as kube-proxy does, balances TCP connections rather than individual requests, so for long-lived or HTTP/2 multiplexed connections you often want a layer-seven balancer or mesh to truly balance request load, and you choose the algorithm to match your request-cost distribution: round-robin for uniform cheap requests, least-connections for variable ones, and consistent hashing when affinity matters.
sections.s3_banking:
The National Bank of India runs several identical transfer-service instances behind a load balancer.

Problem 1 — the team started with plain round-robin, which worked until some transfers triggered slow fraud checks. Round-robin kept sending new requests to an instance already stuck on a slow fraud check, so that instance's latency ballooned while others were underused. This is exactly where least-connections helps: it routes new requests away from the busy instance toward the ones with spare capacity.

Problem 2 — the fleet was mixed, with some instances on larger machines, but round-robin treated them all equally and overloaded the smaller ones. This is exactly where weighted balancing helps: bigger instances get a proportionally larger share.

Problem 3 — a dead instance was still receiving one in N requests and failing them, because there was no health check. This is exactly why health checks must gate the rotation.

The mini-project builds a `LoadBalancer` interface with `RoundRobinBalancer`, `LeastConnectionsBalancer`, and `WeightedRoundRobinBalancer` implementations, plus a `HealthChecker` that removes unhealthy instances. It models each instance tracking its active connections. The demo sends a stream of requests, some slow, under each algorithm, shows round-robin piling onto a busy instance while least-connections balances by load, shows weighted distribution across a mixed fleet, and shows a dead instance being excluded by the health check.

```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the load-balancing demo
java -cp target/classes com.bank.loadbalancer.LoadBalancerDemo

# Kubernetes Service balances automatically across healthy Pods
kubectl apply -f k8s/service.yaml
kubectl get endpoints transfer-service          # shows the healthy Pod IPs in rotation

# For least-request / weighted L7 balancing use a service mesh
istioctl install --set profile=default
# DestinationRule: trafficPolicy.loadBalancer.simple = LEAST_REQUEST
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three identical transfer instances named txn-1, txn-2, txn-3, then a mixed fleet where txn-3 has double capacity, and a scenario where txn-2 fails its health check.

Step 1: Under round-robin with uniform requests, nine requests are dealt out in rotation, so each of the three instances receives exactly three. This is perfectly even when every request costs the same and every instance is identical.

Step 2: The workload turns uneven: txn-1 is stuck handling five slow fraud-check requests, so its active-connection count is high. Round-robin would ignore this and keep feeding txn-1, but we switch to least-connections.

Step 3: Under least-connections, each new request goes to whichever instance currently has the fewest active connections. Because txn-1 is loaded with five, the balancer sends the new work to txn-2 and txn-3 until their load catches up, so txn-1 is avoided while busy. The distribution reflects this, with txn-2 and txn-3 taking the bulk of the new requests.

Step 4: The fleet becomes mixed, with txn-3 on a machine of double capacity, expressed as weight two while txn-1 and txn-2 are weight one. Under weighted round-robin, over eight requests txn-3 receives roughly twice the share of each smaller instance, matching its capacity so the bigger box does proportionally more work.

Step 5: txn-2 fails its health check and is marked unhealthy. The health checker removes it from the eligible list before the balancer ever sees it.

Step 6: Subsequent round-robin distribution draws only from the healthy instances, so requests are served only by txn-1 and txn-3, and none are sent to the dead txn-2. This shows the health check gating the rotation so distribution never includes a failed instance.

```
2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    === Round-robin (uniform) ===
2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    round-robin distribution: {txn-1=3, txn-2=3, txn-3=3}
2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    === Least-connections (uneven load) ===
2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    least-connections distribution: {txn-2=3, txn-3=3} (txn-1 avoided while busy)
2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    === Weighted round-robin (mixed fleet) ===
2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    weighted distribution: {txn-1=2, txn-2=2, txn-3=4} (txn-3 gets ~2x)

2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    after health check, requests served only by: [txn-1, txn-3] (no txn-2)
```

```
┌──────────┐ ┌────────────────┐ ┌────────────────────┐
│RoundRobin│ │LeastConnections│ │WeightedRoundRobin  │
│-counter  │ │(min activeConns)│ │-counter (by weight)│
└──────────┘ └────────────────┘ └────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │     HealthChecker        │ ──────▶│     ServiceInstance      │
  │  + healthyOnly(all)      │        │  - id, weight, healthy   │
  └──────────────────────────┘        │  - activeConnections     │
                                       │  + acquire()/release()   │
                                       └──────────────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: Instance in Rotation ────────────────────────

  [HEALTHY+IDLE] ──acquire──→ [HEALTHY+BUSY] ──release──→ [HEALTHY+IDLE]
        │                                                      ▲
        │ fails health check                                   │ recovers
        ▼                                                      │
   [UNHEALTHY] ───────────────── excluded from choose() ───────┘

  ── Call Chain (least-connections) ─────────────────────────────

  1. healthChecker.healthyOnly(all) → [txn-2, txn-3] (txn-1 busy or txn-2 down)
  2. balancer.choose(healthy)
  3.   → min by activeConnections → txn-2
  4.   → txn-2.acquire() (conns++)
  5. on completion → txn-2.release() (conns--)

  Contract for choose(healthy):
    Pre:  healthy is non-empty (health-filtered)
    Post: returns one instance per the algorithm's rule
    Guarantee: never returns an unhealthy instance
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Distributing requests equally across N instances is the job of a load balancer, which applies a balancing algorithm to pick an instance for each request, and the key is choosing the algorithm that matches your request-cost profile. The simplest is round-robin, which cycles through instances in order and is perfectly fair when requests are uniform and instances are identical. Its weakness is that it ignores how busy each instance actually is, so if one request is slow, round-robin keeps piling new work onto that already-busy instance. That is exactly what happened on our transfer service when some transfers triggered slow fraud checks.

The fix in that case was least-connections, which sends each new request to the instance currently handling the fewest active requests. It adapts naturally to uneven request costs, because an instance stuck on a slow request accumulates connections and is skipped until it catches up. For most real systems, where request durations vary, least-connections is the better default. When the fleet is mixed, with some instances on larger machines, I use weighted variants, where weighted round-robin gives an instance with twice the capacity twice the share, so the bigger boxes do proportionally more work. And when I need affinity, meaning the same key should always hit the same instance, I use consistent hashing, which hashes a key like account id onto a ring so that key sticks to one instance, which helps local caching and sticky sessions, and whose signature benefit is that adding or removing an instance remaps only a small fraction of keys instead of reshuffling everything.

Health checks are what make all of this safe. The load balancer periodically probes each instance and removes any that fail from the rotation, then adds them back on recovery, so traffic is never sent to a dead or warming-up instance. Without health checks, even distribution would blindly include a failed instance and fail a share of requests, which is a bug we hit before adding them.

In Kubernetes most of this is automatic. A Service gives a stable virtual IP and DNS name and tracks the set of healthy Pod endpoints through readiness probes, and kube-proxy spreads requests to the Service across those endpoints, giving round-robin-style balancing at the connection level with no application code. The nuance I always mention is that kube-proxy balances TCP connections rather than individual requests, so for long-lived or HTTP/2 multiplexed connections I put a layer-seven ingress controller or a service mesh in front, where a mesh sidecar can apply least-request balancing and per-route weighting to truly balance request load.

The way I summarize it for an interviewer is that you put a load balancer in front of N stateless, interchangeable instances, you gate the rotation with health checks so only healthy instances receive traffic, and you pick the algorithm to fit the workload: round-robin for uniform cheap requests, least-connections for variable ones, weighted for a mixed-capacity fleet, and consistent hashing when affinity matters. In Kubernetes a Service plus kube-proxy gives you this for free, and a mesh gives you the smarter algorithms when you need them.
